cases.title: Profitable OEM instrument maker, temporary dip, leverage 2.1x, family stake 31%
reasons: Segment fits: Northline designs and builds OEM analyzer systems, which is in-vitro diagnostics instrumentation, one of the segments the strategy targets.
Business model fits: consumables and service are 62% of sales, above the 50% threshold for recurring revenue.
Profitability fits: LTM EBITDA margin is 17%, so the company is profitable, consistent with the strategy's 'profitable mid-sized' requirement.

The price drop looks temporary, not structural: the 38% fall over 12 months follows a two-quarter slip in the launch of the new analyzer platform, which is a product transition. The H1 release shows order intake recovering and first platform shipments completed. The drop is not evidence of a loss of market.
Kill criterion 1 (net debt above 4x EBITDA) is not met: net debt/EBITDA is 2.1x, taken from the data as required.

Kill criterion 2 (a controlling shareholder who ruled out a sale) is not met: the founding family holds 31% and has made no public statement about its stake, so nothing has been ruled out. The 'ruled out' test is passed on the facts given, but the family's intentions remain unknown and should be confirmed.

Ownership flag (required, flag only): Northline Beteiligungs, the founding family vehicle, holds 31% (above the 25% threshold). No public statement about selling has been reported. This is flagged for follow-up, not a reject.

Kill criterion 3 (a major unresolved regulatory issue) is not met: no regulatory matters are reported. This relies on the absence of reported matters, so it should be checked against regulatory filings before any bid.

Good-fit match: the profile closely resembles the thesis's example of a good fit (profitable OEM instrument maker, multi-year supply contracts, share price down after a product transition, founding family holding a large stake).

Limit of this verdict: the profile contains no valuation data. Whether the company can be bought 'at the right price' is not assessed here and is left to the target-price calculation in code, which determines whether the company is Actionable. Priority only means the thesis criteria are met.

Trend check: the 3-month price change is -6%, which suggests the decline is still continuing, even though fundamentals are improving. This is not a thesis criterion, but it should be watched when timing an entry.

Kill criteria, checked one by one: (a) net debt/EBITDA is 3.9x from the data, which is below the 4x threshold, so the kill criterion is not met. (b) No controlling shareholder, so no sale refusal. (c) No regulatory issue reported. No kill criterion is met, so the company is not a Reject.

Leverage headroom is very thin: 0.1x below the 4x kill line. A modest EBITDA miss, or a further debt-funded move, would trigger a Reject. Management's target of 3x within 18 months is guidance, not a result. This is the main risk to the position.

Unknown key fact: the profile gives an EBITDA margin of 19% but no net income or free cash flow. The strategy requires a profitable company, and net profitability cannot be confirmed from the facts. Under the rule that an unknown fact is never a pass, this blocks Priority for now.

Path to Priority: confirm net income and cash generation are positive, confirm from the accounts that the write-down is non-recurring, and track the deleveraging path. The price-target step (ability to pay, takeout price) is handled separately by the code and is not assessed here.

cases.title: Profitable, cheap, but the market is going away
reasons: Segment fits: rapid antigen tests for respiratory viruses are in-vitro diagnostics, one of the segments the thesis likes.

The price drop looks structural, not temporary. Revenue has fallen for three consecutive years as pandemic-era testing volumes disappear, the latest release shows a further 30% decline, and management has no new product with meaningful sales. The thesis lists 'structural decline' as a Radar case, and the 'temporary' test (product transition, destocking, one-off charges) is not met. The share price is down 62% over 12 months, which is consistent with a market that is shrinking rather than one that is temporarily mispricing.

No kill criterion is met. Net debt is 0.4x EBITDA, well below the 4x limit. No controlling shareholder is present: the largest holder is Vanguard at 9%, and insiders hold 4%. The facts report no regulatory issue. Because no kill criterion applies, the verdict is not Reject.
Ownership flag: none required. No holder is above 25%, so there is no sale-willingness question to assess.

Business model is unknown. The facts do not state what share of sales is recurring (consumables, service, supply contracts). Rapid tests are typically sold as one-off product volume, so the recurring-revenue condition is probably not met. This is a warning only and does not change the verdict, but it must not be read as a pass.

Profitability is positive: the LTM EBITDA margin is 24%, supported by cost cuts. The profit is coming from cost reduction on a shrinking top line, which weakens the case for a turnaround that a financing and add-on strategy would fix.

Why not Priority: a thesis criterion is not met (structural rather than temporary decline), and no product cycle is visible that the fund's financing could fund. Buying at the right price requires a recovery thesis that the facts do not support.

What would change the verdict: evidence that the revenue decline is a temporary normalisation of volumes (for example, a stable post-pandemic base with declining rate of fall), a credible new product with meaningful sales, or disclosure that a significant share of sales is recurring under supply contracts. Any of these would support a re-review toward Priority.

cases.title: Good company, wrong segment: medical imaging equipment
reasons: Segment criterion not met: Lumen Imaging makes ultrasound and point-of-care imaging systems for hospitals. The thesis likes in-vitro diagnostics (instruments, assays, OEM analyzers, lab automation). Imaging is in-vivo medical equipment, so this is outside the preferred segments, which the thesis maps to Radar.

Recurring revenue is below the thesis threshold: service contracts are 40% of sales, while the criterion requires recurring revenue to be at least half of sales. This is a warning only and is not a reject, but it is one more thesis criterion not met, so Priority is not available.

Kill criteria checked, none met: (a) net debt is 1.8x EBITDA, below the 4x limit, using the figure from the data; (b) there is no controlling shareholder, so none has ruled out a sale; (c) the facts state there is no regulatory issue. Because no kill criterion is met, Reject does not apply.

The price drop looks temporary, as the thesis requires. The shares fell 33% over 12 months (-7% over 3 months) after a delayed UK hospital tender cycle, which management expects to resume. This is a timing effect, not a structural loss of market. Still, it is management's expectation, not independently verified, so it should be confirmed.
Ownership: the largest holder is Baillie Gifford at 11%, and insiders hold 6%. No holder exceeds the 25% flag threshold, so there is nothing to flag and no public statement on selling to assess.

Known gaps that keep this from a stronger verdict: the profile gives EBITDA margin (16%) but not net income or free cash flow, so 'profitable' is only partly evidenced. The profile also does not say whether the company is a pure OEM supplier or sells direct to hospitals, which matters for the 'OEM analyzers' fit. Both should be checked before any reconsideration.

Overall: the company passes all kill criteria and has a plausibly temporary drop, but it fails the segment criterion and the recurring-revenue criterion. Under the thesis rules that makes it Radar: keep watching. It would only move to Priority if the business were shown to be in-vitro diagnostics with recurring revenue of at least 50%, which the current facts do not support.
